issue: 'Prolegomena' is an obscure scholarly term with no help; a listener will not know it is a book title/genre.
find: once his Prolegomena to some branch
replace: once his Prolegomena, his scholarly introduction, to some branch

issue: Paragraph opens 'It flattered him' straight after a paragraph about Mr. Carmichael's marriage; the 'him' (Tansley) is not clear until three sentences later.
find: It flattered him. After being snubbed
replace: It flattered Tansley. After being snubbed

issue: Archaic colon-plus-dash punctuation ':—' is distracting on the page and meaningless aloud.
find: it was this: it was this:—she was
replace: it was this: it was this—she was

issue: Chapter 1 ended in the town with Tansley carrying her bag; chapter 2 cuts back to the window with a bare 'he said'. First-time readers may assume Mr. Ramsay (who said the same thing in 1.2). Naming the speaker costs nothing; 2.1 keeps the 'hateful little man' judgement.
find: “No going to the Lighthouse, James,” he said, as he stood
replace: “No going to the Lighthouse, James,” Charles Tansley said, as he stood

issue: New chapter switches to Lily's viewpoint but opens with 'he nearly knocked her easel over'; after chapter 3 ended on Mrs. Ramsay bowing her head, 'her' reads as Mrs. Ramsay and 'he' is unanchored until mid-paragraph.
find: Indeed, he nearly knocked her easel over
replace: Indeed, Mr. Ramsay nearly knocked Lily’s easel over

issue: 'He was done' reads in modern idiom as 'he was finished/defeated', not 'he had finished thinking'.
find: That was it. He was done.
replace: That was it. He had finished.

issue: First mention of 'Sorley' with no link; so far the child has only been 'the Lighthouse keeper’s little boy'. A listener meets an unknown name.
find: even allowing for the fact that Sorley’s little boy would be
replace: even allowing for the fact that Sorley’s little boy, the Lighthouse keeper’s son, would be

issue: British spelling 'moulded' breaks the edition's American spelling (the quotation is Bankes's own speech, not verse).
'fell as a thunderbolt' uses archaic 'fell' (= fierce/deadly); every modern reader and listener hears the verb 'fell', which contradicts the charge image and garbles the sentence.
find: as he rode, fell as a thunderbolt, fierce as a hawk
replace: as he rode, deadly as a thunderbolt, fierce as a hawk

issue: Tennyson refrain inconsistent: 3.7 (and Tennyson) have 'Stormed at with shot and shell'; here 'by'.
find: Stormed at by shot and shell
replace: Stormed at with shot and shell

issue: 'his father ... his youngest son' in one clause is hard to parse aloud (whose father/son?), and 'spray' contradicts 'sprig' in 6.4/6.5.
find: the tickling spray with which his father was teasing his youngest son’s bare leg
replace: the tickling sprig with which Mr. Ramsay was teasing his youngest son’s bare leg

issue: 'forlorn hope' is an obsolete military term (a storming party sent ahead to near-certain death); modern readers take it as 'a hopeless wish', which makes 'the leader of a forlorn hope' nonsense.
find: Surely the leader of a forlorn hope has the right
replace: Surely the leader of a forlorn hope, a doomed advance party, has the right

issue: 'he' follows a paragraph ending on James and the 'like a child' simile points to James too; the referent is Mr. Ramsay.
find: like a child who falls asleep contented, he looked at her
replace: like a child who falls asleep contented, Mr. Ramsay looked at her

issue: Inconsistent term: 'Grimm’s fairy tale' in 7.5, then capitalized 'the Fairy Tale' here as if it were a title.
find: she went back to the Fairy Tale
replace: she went back to the fairy tale

issue: 'she turned him out of the room': in a paragraph told from Mrs. Ramsay's view, 'she' reads as Mrs. Ramsay; it is Carmichael's wife.
find: and she turned him out of the room
replace: and his wife turned him out of the room

issue: Sentence does not parse ('The way Lily saw him gazing ... was a rapture').
find: The way Lily saw him gazing at Mrs. Ramsay was a rapture that matched
replace: Watching him gaze at Mrs. Ramsay, Lily saw a rapture that matched

issue: 'her painting' comes in a run where 'she/her' switches between Lily and Mrs. Ramsay several times; here it means Lily's.
find: didn’t care a fig about her painting
replace: didn’t care a fig about Lily’s painting

issue: 'Lily had her sense of her back now' reads aloud as Lily sensing Mrs. Ramsay's (or her own) physical back; meaning is 'Lily had recovered her sense of Mrs. Ramsay'.
find: Lily had her sense of her back now
replace: Lily had got back her sense of Mrs. Ramsay now

issue: 'That meant he meant' is a clumsy echo that trips a narrator.
find: That meant he meant to catch crabs
replace: That meant he intended to catch crabs

issue: After two paragraphs deep in Mrs. Ramsay's solitude, 'He turned' needs an anchor; the last 'he' was two paragraphs back.
replace: Mr. Ramsay turned and saw her.

issue: 'find it' directly follows 'he had once found a gold watch', so 'it' reads as the watch, not Minta's brooch.
find: and he was certain he’d find it.
replace: and he was certain he’d find the brooch.

issue: 'every feeling felt for yourself' reads as self-pity; the sense is feelings other people have for you (Rose's feeling for her mother).
find: Like every feeling felt for yourself, Mrs. Ramsay thought,
replace: Like every feeling that someone has for you, Mrs. Ramsay thought,

issue: 'the man in the drainpipe' is a new, odd image; in 1.27 it was a man digging in a drain who looked at her.
find: the man in the drainpipe gazing up at her
replace: the man digging in the drain gazing up at her

issue: Grammatical hole: 'making a note that some day he would read aloud' has no object.
find: making a note that some day he would read aloud to a friend or two
replace: making a note of it to read aloud some day to a friend or two

issue: 'their duty ... to help us' follows a sentence about the woman's duty, so 'their' reads as women; it means men.
find: Just as it is their duty, she thought,
replace: Just as it is men’s duty, she thought,

issue: Inconsistent term: Tansley's father is 'a chemist' who 'keeps a shop' in 1.20, a 'pharmacist' here; readers may think two facts are being given.
replace: his father a chemist with a shop

issue: Generic lighthouse capitalized; 17.26 has 'a lighthouse' lowercase, and the capital L is reserved for the Lighthouse.
find: how long do they keep men on a Lighthouse?
replace: how long do they keep men on a lighthouse?

issue: 'He remarked' after Mrs. Ramsay speaks: the last 'he' in the scene was Tansley; it is Mr. Bankes.
'What had she done with it?' — 'she' reads as Mrs. Ramsay herself; it is Rose, named only in the next sentence.
find: What had she done with it? Mrs. Ramsay wondered.
replace: What had Rose done with it? Mrs. Ramsay wondered.

issue: Refrain drift: the brief's recurring motif is 'the thing is made that endures'; here it becomes 'remains forever after', which will not echo in Part III.
find: that the thing is made that remains forever after. This would remain.
replace: that the thing is made that endures. This would endure.

issue: Hyphenation inconsistent with chapters 1–17, which write 'drawing room' as a noun.
find: the smoking-room, the drawing-room or up
replace: the smoking room, the drawing room, or up

issue: Hyphenated noun 'drawing-room' inconsistent with 'drawing room' elsewhere.
Refrain inconsistency: the Luriana Lurilee line was 'buzzing with the yellow bee' in 17.66; here 'honey bee'. Check the source: if Woolf varies it herself, keep; otherwise align.
